subChunks.title: Measuring Before Optimising: Benchmarking & Profiling Basics
subChunks.hookHtml: Performance problems are almost always in the 3% of code you'd never guess. That's why Donald Knuth's warning — 'premature optimisation is the root of all evil' — still holds. The discipline of performance tuning starts with measurement, not intuition.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Performance Tuning Process

  1. Establish a baseline: measure current performance under representative load
  2. Profile: find where time is actually spent (CPU, memory, I/O, blocking)
  3. Identify the bottleneck: only fix what the profiler shows is hot
  4. Change one thing: isolate cause and effect
  5. Re-measure: confirm the improvement and check for regressions

Microbenchmarking Pitfalls

Naively timing code with System.nanoTime() produces unreliable results due to JIT warmup, dead-code elimination, and CPU frequency scaling. The JVM optimises hot paths after thousands of executions — your first measurement captures cold performance.

// BAD — JIT hasn't warmed up; results meaningless
long start = System.nanoTime();
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) expensiveOperation();
long ns = System.nanoTime() - start;
System.out.println(ns / 1000 + " µs");

// BETTER — warm up first, then measure
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) expensiveOperation(); // warmup
long start = System.nanoTime();
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) expensiveOperation(); // measurement
long ns = System.nanoTime() - start;
System.out.printf("%.2f µs per op%n", (double) ns / 100_000 / 1000);

JMH — Java Microbenchmark Harness

The correct tool for microbenchmarks. JMH handles warmup, multi-iteration averaging, dead-code elimination prevention, and OS scheduling noise. Add to pom.xml:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.openjdk.jmh</groupId>
    <artifactId>jmh-core</artifactId>
    <version>1.37</version>
</dependency>
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.MICROSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5)
@Measurement(iterations = 10)
public class StringBench {
    @Benchmark
    public String concatenation() {
        String s = "";
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) s += i;  // creates 100 new objects
        return s;
    }

    @Benchmark
    public String builder() {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) sb.append(i);
        return sb.toString();
    }
}

Common Performance Patterns

String concatenation in loops: each += creates a new String. Use StringBuilder.

Boxing/unboxing: using Integer instead of int in hot code adds allocation and GC pressure. Use primitives in tight loops.

Collection initial capacity: new ArrayList<>(expectedSize) prevents repeated resizing and copying.

Lazy initialisation: compute expensive values only when first needed; cache the result.

Cache-friendly access: arrays have better CPU cache locality than linked structures — prefer arrays or ArrayList over LinkedList.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's spell execution pipeline could cast 800 spells per second in testing. Under real tournament load it slumped to 120. Two weeks of guessing produced nothing. One afternoon with a profiler pinpointed a single method: the spell name formatter, called 2 million times per second, rebuilding a regular expression Pattern on every call.

storyBeats.speaker: Performance Sage Torben
storyBeats.text: Performance problems hide. The obvious places are rarely the bottleneck. I have seen developers spend a week rewriting a sorting algorithm that ran for 12 milliseconds in a service that spent 4 seconds waiting for a database query. The profiler would have told them in five minutes.

storyBeats.speaker: Performance Sage Torben
storyBeats.text: JMH is non-negotiable for benchmarks. System.nanoTime in a loop tells you what the JVM does before it optimises your code, not after. In production, the JIT has run for hours and the code is maximally hot. A cold benchmark is measuring a completely different thing.

storyBeats.speaker: Pattern compilation — the hidden allocator
Performance Sage Torben
storyBeats.text: Three things account for 80% of Java performance problems I have seen: N+1 database queries, Pattern.compile() inside a hot method, and String concatenation in a loop. All trivially fixable once measured. Profile first. Always.

learningObjectives: Explain why naïve System.nanoTime benchmarks are unreliable and what JMH solves
Describe the five-step performance tuning process: baseline, profile, identify, change, re-measure
Identify and fix the three most common Java performance anti-patterns (String concatenation, boxing, Pattern compilation)
Calculate throughput and latency from timing measurements and express in correct units
commonMistakes: Optimising before measuring — fixing code that is not the bottleneck while the real bottleneck remains
Benchmarking without warmup — measuring JIT compilation time rather than steady-state performance
Changing multiple things between measurements — makes it impossible to know what actually helped
Using LinkedList thinking it is faster for insert-at-middle — ArrayList is faster in almost all real workloads due to cache locality
assessmentCriteria: Can explain what JIT warmup is and why it makes cold benchmarks misleading
Can rewrite a string-concatenation loop to use StringBuilder and explain the allocation saving
Can identify Pattern.compile() inside a hot method as a performance bug and extract it to a static field
Can describe the five steps of performance tuning in order and explain why 'measure first' is step 1
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a developer why their intuition about which code is slow is probably wrong, and walk them through how you would actually find the bottleneck in a production Java service.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write a PerfDemo class that demonstrates two performance comparisons with simple timed measurements (warm up 10,000 iterations, then measure 100,000 iterations):

  1. Compare String += concatenation vs StringBuilder.append() — build a string of 50 numbers in each case. Print both times in nanoseconds.
  2. Demonstrate static Pattern compilation — write two methods: matchBad(String s) using s.matches(...) and matchGood(String s) using a static compiled Pattern. Confirm both return the same boolean result for an input of your choice.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Write a class BoxingPerf that demonstrates the cost of boxing in a hot loop. Write two methods: long sumBoxed(int n) that sums 0..n-1 using an Integer accumulator (not int), and long sumPrimitive(int n) that uses a plain int. Warm up 10,000 times each, then time 1,000,000 iterations of each with n=1000. Print both times and confirm results are identical. Also print the GC observation: 'boxed allocates per addition; primitive does not'.

questions.questionHtml: Why does calling String.matches(regex) inside a hot loop cause a performance problem?
options: It compiles a new Pattern object on every call
The method is synchronized and causes thread contention
questions.correctAnswer: It compiles a new Pattern object on every call
questions.explanationHtml: String.matches(regex) internally calls Pattern.compile(regex).matcher(this).matches() — creating and discarding a new Pattern on every invocation. Pattern compilation is expensive. The fix: compile once to a static final Pattern and reuse the matcher.

questions.questionHtml: A benchmark shows LinkedList.get(index) is 100× slower than ArrayList.get(index). Why?
options: LinkedList.get() traverses from the head node — O(n) vs ArrayList's O(1) index
ArrayList is backed by a hash table
questions.correctAnswer: LinkedList.get() traverses from the head node — O(n) vs ArrayList's O(1) index
questions.explanationHtml: ArrayList stores elements in a contiguous array — index access is O(1) and CPU-cache-friendly. LinkedList is a doubly-linked list — get(n) traverses up to n/2 nodes. For most workloads (including insert-at-middle), ArrayList wins due to cache locality. LinkedList's advantage (O(1) insert at an iterator position) rarely matters in practice.

questions.questionHtml: A System.nanoTime benchmark without a warmup phase accurately reflects the performance of JIT-optimised production code.
questions.explanationHtml: Without warmup, you measure code before JIT compilation has converted hot bytecode to native machine code. Production code that has been running for hours is maximally optimised. Cold measurements can be 10–100× slower than steady-state JIT performance, producing completely misleading benchmark results.
